items_missed: No real agenda statement. 'Do you have just a few moments to go over that and make sure the accurate?' set a purpose but no roadmap and no timeframe — the customer was never told she would gather details, then get walked through pricing, or that it would take 10-15 minutes. She also answered her own question ('Alright, awesome') before Madeleine's 'I sure do' landed.

Save Your Ass section scored zero — the entire prep speech is absent. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples (kids' toys, garden tools, loose items in drawers, photos off walls), no 'take a carload' tip. This is the single largest point loss on the call and the most expensive one for estimate accuracy, because the whole job is 15-25 boxes of loose apartment contents where consolidation is exactly the lever.
Declared the estimate accurate before gathering a single detail: 'Alright, awesome estimate is accurate' came in the opening breath, ahead of every probe question.

Then found a material change to the job and never revisited the estimate. The online form said the destination was a one-story house; Madeleine corrected it live — 'the part that I'm on is like a lower suite of a larger building... it still requires like a walking down some stairs' and 'pretty much the stairs are the only access.' Bri said 'Okay' and moved on. Stairs-only destination access on a 3.5-hour system estimate was never re-checked, never flagged to the customer, and there is no indication it was corrected in EMMA.

Never converted hours to dollars. The customer got '$208 for two movers' and 'about three and a half hours' as separate facts and was never given the actual estimated total (~$728), so she has no number to plan against.

The estimate range was delivered garbled and self-contradicting: 'the system estimated, you about three and a half hours a typical move besides usually takes between 23 and a half or two and a half to three and a half hours' — the system number sat at the top of a range she described as typical, which quietly tells the customer 3.5 hours is the worst case when the stairs make it the likely floor.

Variables gathered but never explained. She collected the 4th-floor elevator, the 50-foot walks at both ends, the stairs-only destination, the six-piece sectional and the 'somewhat substantial wood dresser' — and never told the customer how any of it moves the clock.
Disassembly / reassembly never mentioned, on a move with a mattress, a one-bedroom setup, and a substantial wood dresser. No 'assembly fees' in the no-hidden-fees list either.
'Everything is included in that hourly rate' with no itemization — gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands and tools were never named, so the customer can't tell what 'everything' covers.
No deposit required was never mentioned — a core Einstein differentiator, skipped entirely.

Email handoff explained but not framed: no mention of the bolded key details at the top, and no 'reply with any corrections so we can verify' — 'reply to the email' was offered only for questions. Business hours never given.
Never asked about packing services, additional rooms (garage, storage unit, balcony), additional stops, or a storage stop.

The stressor probe was asked and then dropped. 'Do you have any questions or concerns specifically about this move?' drew 'No, not really,' and Bri went straight to 'Okay, great' with no second attempt anywhere in the call to surface what Madeleine was actually worried about.
Customer's name used once as an address ('may I speak with Madeline?') — the only other occurrence is spelling her email back. Short of the 3+ standard.

No 60 cents per pound baseline alongside No Worries, so the customer has no reference point for why $2,000 of coverage matters. Also called it 'free evaluation coverage' rather than valuation coverage.

The pricing, no-hidden-fees, clock and three-differentiator block was delivered as one unbroken monologue with a single 'Does that all make sense?' at the end — no pauses or checkpoints across roughly 90 seconds of the most important content on the call.
top_strength: Bri ran the tightest, most disciplined intake in this batch — 5.8 minutes with essentially no wasted motion, and she caught two things the online form had wrong. She refused to accept a soft number on walk distance and pushed until it was real: 'And then how close is your apartment from the elevator to the apartment,' which got her the useful breakdown 'it's probably like ten feet to the elevator from like a good parking spot and then the rest is forty feet from the elevator to the apartment,' and later she said plainly 'you said fifty feet, do you feel like it's fifty or more? Like a hundred. I can't really tell on the Google' rather than guessing off the map. She also anchored the box count instead of asking an open question — 'typical move this size has about fifteen to 25 boxes. Do you feel like you fall within that range?' — which is the right technique and got a confident answer. And the differentiator block was complete and accurate on all three: No Worries quoted correctly at 'up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse for accidental damages,' Meet Your Mover with the real reason behind it ('our movers are not daily contracted workers... helping ease [the tension] of strangers arriving at your front door'), and the On-Time Guarantee with the actual mechanic ('if we can't make it in the time window that we arranged, we immediately start discounting money of your bill'). All four clock bullets were hit cleanly. This rep knows the script; she is skipping sections, not fumbling them.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is the Save Your Ass speech, which is missing entirely and is worth ten points and real hours on this specific job. After confirming the box count Bri should have said: 'Madeleine, one thing that saves people the most money — everything the movers can pick up and carry as a single item goes faster, so if you can get loose stuff out of drawers and off the walls and into boxes before Thursday, and take a carload of the small awkward things over yourself, that comes straight off the clock and straight off your bill. Does that make sense?' On a 15-to-25-box apartment with a 40-foot elevator walk, that speech is the difference between the 2.5-hour end of her range and the 3.5-hour end. Second priority, and the one that matters most to the estimate-accuracy rock: she uncovered a genuine estimate breaker and let it pass. Madeleine told her the destination is a lower suite where 'the stairs are the only access,' contradicting the one-story house on the form. The line needed was 'Okay, that's a change from what we have on file — the form said one story with no stairs, and stairs-only access at the drop-off usually adds time, so let me note that on the job. With the stairs and the forty-foot elevator walk on the front end I'd plan on the upper end of that range, closer to three and a half hours, which at $208 an hour is about $730.' Instead she said 'Okay' twice and moved on, and the customer walked away with a number that may not survive move day. Third: she never gave a dollar total and never said there's no deposit — two sentences that cost nothing and are the reason people book with Einstein. Fourth: break the monologue. The pricing-plus-clock-plus-differentiators run had one sense-check at the very end; put a checkpoint after pricing and another after the clock so the customer is still with her. Business item to fix today: confirm the destination stairs-only access is logged in EMMA on the September 10 job so dispatch and the crew aren't finding out on arrival.
phone_presence_notes: Polite, efficient and warm at the close ('You're so welcome. Have a good rest of your day'), and the customer stayed positive throughout ('that all sounds great,' 'Thank you so much') — but the language was scripted and transactional, the name was used once, there was no humor or rapport moment, and Madeleine's answers stayed monosyllabic ('Mm-hmm,' 'Yeah,' 'Okay') because nothing invited more.
audio_review_reason: Several stretches are transcribed badly enough that pace and clarity can't be judged from text — 'This is bra calling from Einstein moving,' 'no sterle. Fees,' and the estimate range rendered as '23 and a half or two and a half to three and a half hours' — and the opening shows overlapping speech ('Alright, awesome estimate is accurate' printed before the customer's 'I sure do'), so whether she actually talked over the customer needs the audio to confirm.
